judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2102, which would have required every Iowa driver's license test to be given in English. The state and the private testers it uses could no longer test an applicant in another language. The bill took driver's license tests out of an exception to Iowa's law that makes English the official language of state business. The Iowa House passed it 58-30, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2133, which would have listed kratom, a plant sold in shops as a supplement, as a Schedule I controlled substance. That is the class for drugs the state treats as having a high risk of abuse and no accepted medical use. Possessing kratom would have been a serious misdemeanor the first time and a felony after two earlier convictions. Before the vote, the House rejected, 44-51, an amendment to regulate kratom sales instead of banning it. The Iowa House passed it 69-26, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 269, which would have barred Iowa's three public universities from requiring students to take a course with diversity, equity, and inclusion or critical race theory content to meet any degree requirement. That content included the idea that race-neutral laws keep oppression in place, or that a student is biased because of race or sex. Universities also could not require or reward faculty for teaching that content or attending such training. The Board of Regents could exempt programs focused on racial, ethnic, or gender studies. The Iowa House passed it 63-34, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2487, which would have given the attorney general new power to enforce Iowa's existing ban on diversity, equity, and inclusion offices and practices in state and local government and at public colleges. The attorney general could investigate, demand records by subpoena, and hire outside lawyers, with the government body or college paying their fees. By fall 2028 the Board of Regents would also have had to review required university courses for such content and could order them dropped. The Iowa House passed it 62-27, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2488, which would have barred private colleges whose students receive Iowa Tuition Grants, the state's aid for students at private colleges, from running a diversity, equity, and inclusion office unless federal or state law or accreditation rules required one. Teaching, research, student groups, and health services were not covered. Anyone could report a college to the attorney general. A college that did not fix a violation within 30 days would have lost access to the tuition grant program the next school year. The Iowa House passed it 57-34, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2513, which would have barred Iowa's public universities, community colleges, and private colleges from hiring certain holders of an H-1B visa, the federal work visa for skilled foreign professionals. From July 2026 on, they could not hire an H-1B holder who is a citizen of a country the federal government names as a foreign adversary or a state sponsor of terrorism. The Iowa House passed it 68-27, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2529, which would have required makers of diesel farm equipment to give owners the repair information, software updates, replacement parts, and diagnostic tools for the machine's diesel exhaust fluid system on the same terms they offer their authorized dealers. That system uses a fluid to cut nitrogen oxide pollution. Makers could not require their approval before a part or tool is used. Breaking the rules would have been an unfair trade practice, and contract terms waiving them would have been void. The Iowa House passed it 57-33, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2557, which would have said that raising a child in a way consistent with the child's sex is not child abuse or child endangerment. That covered using names and pronouns that match the child's sex, seeking counseling to help the child live consistent with it, and refusing consent to gender transition care. The state could not deny a foster care license or an adoption for that reason, and a court could not count it against a parent in a custody case. The Iowa House passed it 65-31, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2584, which would have made the area within 300 feet of a homeless shelter or housing program that gets government money a drug-free zone. Selling drugs there would have added a year to the sentence, with no probation, and a fine of at least $2,000. A shelter operator who let clients have or use illegal drugs on site would have committed an aggravated misdemeanor and could have lost state homelessness grants for three years. The Iowa House passed it 70-21, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2624, which would have required people arrested for a felony or a violent aggravated misdemeanor to give a DNA sample for the state database. Iowa law takes a sample only after a conviction or a deferred judgment. The DNA record would have been erased automatically within 30 days if the charge was dismissed, the person was acquitted, or no charge was filed within a year of the arrest. The record would have stayed if the person owed a DNA sample for another case or it was evidence in another investigation. The Iowa House passed it 64-30, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2718, which would have barred state and local agencies and police from enforcing any red flag law, including federal orders. The bill defined a red flag law as any order or rule that takes guns from, or bars guns for, someone not convicted of a violent felony or otherwise disqualified under Iowa law. Agencies could not take federal money to enforce such laws. An agency whose officer knowingly enforced one would have faced a $50,000 civil penalty for each case and could have been sued. The Iowa House passed it 67-29, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 546, which would have set a minimum bond of $100,000 at the first court appearance for six violent or gun crimes when the arrest is made on a warrant. They were attempted murder, assault with a weapon, willful injury, intimidation with a dangerous weapon, going armed with intent, and gun possession by a felon. People arrested for these crimes also could not be released under the standard bail schedule used when courts are closed. The Iowa House passed it 64-31, but the full Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.
